paras: The Monroe County stake burning was the killing of an unnamed man, one of two lodgers who gave the name Miller, by a crowd that burned him at a stake in northern Monroe County, Mississippi, in December 1880. He was accused of chloroforming, robbing and burning to death a young farmer, Brown Riding, with his wife and two-year-old daughter. Tupelo dispatches spread the story nationally, and northern editors argued over whether the burning was fitting punishment or murder.

Riding, described as a young man raised in the neighborhood, had married and built a cottage near his parents, about twenty miles from Tupelo. On the disagreeable night of Saturday, December 18, two men giving the name Miller asked to stay the night and were given a bed in the family's only room with a fireplace. Around eleven o'clock neighbors saw the cottage in flames, and the charred remains of all three family members were later found in the ruins.

Searchers found that the two lodgers had separated, one heading toward Aberdeen and the other toward Tupelo. A posse found the Aberdeen-bound man hiding in a field six miles from that town, and according to the Picayune's correspondent he was carrying nine dollars, Riding's watch, a suit of clothes and boots. Taken back to the scene, he reportedly confessed that the pair had chloroformed the sleeping family, taken $27 and the valuables, and fired cotton soaked in coal oil.

The crowd then pinioned him, piled pine splinters around him and set him ablaze. The Memphis wire put the crowd at 'twenty-five resolute men', while the Tupelo special to the Picayune said seventy-five men fastened him to a stake. A dispatch dated December 20 described the burning as having taken place 'last night', which would place it on December 19.

The other man was still being sought at last report, and the wire predicted he would 'share the same fate if caught'. No report of an inquest, arrests among the crowd, or the second man's capture appears in the coverage. The Picayune version added that a similar crime had happened in the same neighborhood four years earlier.

Mississippi papers ran the Tupelo specials with headlines such as 'Fiendish Murderers' and 'One of the Perpetrators Burned at the Stake', calling the triple murder the most diabolical episode in the state's history. The Jackson Weekly Clarion's text said the man was 'permitted to die the death he had so mercilessly meted to his benefactors'. From December 22 the Memphis wire appeared in the New-York Tribune, the Portland Daily Press and other northern and western papers, under headlines like 'Terrible Punishment for a Crime' and 'Retribution in Mississippi'.

Northern editorial comment divided. The Sacramento Daily Record-Union said the twenty-five 'substantial citizens' had become 'murderers themselves'. The Butler Citizen in Pennsylvania instead approved, pairing the case with the recent lynching of Snyder in that state. The Delaware State Journal used the same comparison to rebuke the Norristown Herald, which had cited the burning as proof of Mississippi barbarism.
Only the National Republican's version gave a race, calling the two lodgers 'two white men'.

Beyond the crowd size, accounts differ on the family's name, printed as 'Brown Riding' in most copies but as 'Mr. Brown' or 'the Brown family' in others. The Clarion placed the capture near 'Evergreen' rather than Aberdeen, and a Memphis dispatch of December 21 also used 'last night', which would put the burning on December 20.

reader.title: Monroe County, Mississippi, stake burning (1880)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd of 25 or 75 men burned a captured man at a stake at the scene of the crime he was accused of, without any legal process (A1, A6, A9).

The man was burned to death by a crowd of 'twenty-five resolute men' (A1, A4) or 'seventy-five' (A5, A6), with no officer or court involved, as punishment for the alleged murder of the Riding (Brown) family (A1, A2).
Two separate Tupelo specials, one to the Memphis Avalanche (A10, A1) and one to the New Orleans Picayune (A6, A5), agree on the crime, capture and burning while differing on crowd size.

accounts.label: Memphis Avalanche special (Tupelo)
accounts.gist: Two men named Miller lodged with the Ridings, chloroformed and robbed them, and fired the house; one was found hiding near Aberdeen, confessed at the scene, and 25 men burned him.

accounts.label: New Orleans Picayune special (Tupelo)
accounts.gist: Same crime; $9, Riding's watch, clothes and boots were found on the captive, and 75 men fastened him to a stake with fat pine.

accounts.label: Northern editorials
accounts.gist: The Sacramento Record-Union called the lynchers murderers; the Butler Citizen approved; the Delaware State Journal defended Mississippi against the Norristown Herald.

framing.detail: Mississippi specials headlined 'Fiendish Murderers' and 'One of the Perpetrators Burned at the Stake' and said he was 'permitted to die the death he had so mercilessly meted' out.
Northern dailies ran the Memphis wire under heads such as 'Terrible Punishment for a Crime' and 'Retribution in Mississippi'.
The Sacramento Record-Union said the 25 'substantial citizens' had become 'murderers themselves'.
The Butler Citizen said the burning did not lower 'the dignity of the common law'.
The Delaware State Journal called it 'a horrible crime ... horribly punished' but used it to rebut a Pennsylvania paper's attack on Mississippi.
